1. A stronger chemical construction

The most promising direction is no longer a photocage containing two simultaneously generated radicals. It is a chemically stored reaction partner that can be activated and consumed at different times.

I am selecting the formation of carbon–carbon bonds between primary and tertiary alkyl fragments, particularly the quaternary carbon centres important in pharmaceutical synthesis.

ASTRA — Chemical transformation: From fragment storage to selective reaction control
1. A decisive limitation of the Fe(OEP) construction

The strongest new conclusion is that a stored Fe–alkyl intermediate does not automatically create useful programmable chemistry. Its value depends on what can be done after loading that cannot be achieved just as effectively by conventional feed scheduling.

The primary experimental foundation is sound within its scope. Pace and colleagues demonstrated Fe(I)(OEP) activation of primary alkyl electrophiles, accumulation of a primary Fe(III)–alkyl intermediate, and productive coupling with tertiary radicals under iron/photoredox conditions. The reaction also works with primary mesylates, not only alkyl bromides. 
macmillan.princeton.edu

To process an entire batch after its precursor supply has disappeared, the architecture requires either approximately stoichiometric storage capacity or repeated transfer of precursor into a larger reservoir.

This is not a limitation on ordinary catalytic turnover. A catalyst can turn over many times when fresh precursor remains available. It is specifically a limit on how much molecular identity can be retained across a period when the precursor is no longer available.

The published Fe(OEP) reaction used 10 mol% iron in its standard conditions, with reactions commonly illuminated for 24 hours. It establishes multiple catalytic turnovers, but not a stoichiometric inventory of persistent Fe–alkyl.
